title: Seasonal variance gave no clear six-month Pacific volume probability forecast gain at 2000-2023 origins
abstract: We tested whether seasonal error variance improves six-month forecasts of Pacific basin warm water volume change. Fixed NOAA GODAS and CPC ERSSTv5 snapshots supplied 288 monthly origins in 2000-2023. Both Gaussian rules used identical earlier-only mean forecasts with seasonal state slopes and a Pacific temperature contrast. An annual cycle in log variance reduced mean continuous ranked probability score from 0.421339 to 0.420686, or 0.155%. The conditional 95% three-year block interval was -0.141% to +0.447%. One- and five-year blocks, two record halves, a second variance harmonic and a mean model without the temperature contrast also left gains uncertain. Overall central 80% coverage was 80.903% for both rules. This test gives no clear seasonal uncertainty gain for this target and model. It does not show absent seasonal dynamics. Few cycles, revised data, Gaussian errors, training fit residuals and conditional intervals limit inference. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, checks and a figure are included.

display.caption: Six-month volume change forecast scores and central 80% coverage by origin month. Lower CRPS is better. Each month has 24 test observations. The primary overall score reduction interval includes zero.

citations.reason: We use its mean model, source snapshots and test years with new code. Shared data do not give independent confirmation.
Prior seasonal variance test had a temperature target and earlier forecast-error calibration. We test volume change with training fit residuals.
